```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(F2Adonis2)
```


## Summary

F2Adonis2 is an R package designed for reliable multivariate analysis of variance using distance matrices. It implements the $F_2$ statistic as proposed by Anderson et al. (2017) to provide a solution to the multivariate Behrens-Fisher problem (BFP). The BFP arises when researchers need to test the null hypothesis of equality of mean vectors (centroids) across two or more populations while their dispersion matrices (variances) differ.

## Statement of Need

In multivariate ecological and biological studies, researchers often rely on distance-based permutational methods like PERMANOVA (the $F_1$ statistic) to detect differences among groups. However, standard PERMANOVA is strictly valid only when group dispersions are homogeneous. As demonstrated in Anderson et al. (2017), the $F_1$ test is not reliable under heterogeneous dispersions in the space of the chosen dissimilarity measure, particularly for unbalanced designs:

Inflated Type I Error: When smaller groups have larger spreads, the $F_1$ test becomes too liberal, falsely identifying differences in centroids.

Loss of Power: When larger groups have larger spreads, the $F_1$ test becomes too conservative.

F2Adonis2 provides a mathematically grounded solution by modifying the PERMANOVA test statistic, ensuring valid inference even when groups exhibit heteroskedasticity in non-Euclidean space.

## Methodology: The $F_2$ Statistic

The $F_2$ statistic addresses the BFP by replacing the pooled residual error term in the denominator with a weighted sum of group-specific mean-squared dissimilarities ($V_i$):

$$F_2 = \frac{SS_A}{\sum_{i=1}^g (1 - n_i/N)V_i}$$

Where $SS_A$ is the among-group sum of squares, $g$ is the number of groups, $n_i$ is the sample size of group $i$, $N$ is the total sample size, and $V_i$ is the group-specific variance calculated in dissimilarity space.

### Resampling Methods

By default, $p$-values are computed by permuting group labels and recalculating the group-specific dispersions $V_i$ for every permutation. The package also provides separate-sample residual bootstrapping (`bootstrap = TRUE`), which resamples residuals within each group in centered dissimilarity space so the groups share a common centroid, along with an empirical bias adjustment for the resulting bootstrap variances (`bias.adjust = TRUE`). Following Anderson et al. (2017), permutation is recommended for general applications, since it gave better Type I error control and equal or greater power than the bootstrap in their simulations.

## Univariate Comparison

The test statistic provides a generalization of Welch's F-test. The following code compares Welch's F-test with the conventional ANOVA in a situation with no difference in the means but different variances.

```{r}
################################################################################
# F2Adonis2 Vignette: Univariate Validation and Welch's F Comparison
################################################################################

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(vegan)
library(F2Adonis2)
library(onewaytests)

# ==============================================================================
# 1. Simulate three unbalanced groups, same means, different variances:
# ==============================================================================
set.seed(93939)
Xf <- factor(c(rep("Lev1", 15), rep("Lev2", 10), rep("Lev3", 5)))
y1 <- rnorm(n = 30, mean = rep(0, 30), sd = 20 * as.numeric(Xf))
df1 <- data.frame(y1, Xf)

# Visualize the heterogeneity (The Behrens-Fisher Problem)
df1 %>% ggplot(aes(x = Xf, y = y1, fill = Xf)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Simulation: Same Means, Heterogeneous Variance")

# Standard ANOVA - Strong evidence (p=0.031) because it is biased by the variance
anova(lm(y1 ~ Xf, data = df1))

# ==============================================================================
# 2. Welch's F-test and Permutational Null
# ==============================================================================
welch_res <- oneway.test(y1 ~ Xf, data = df1)
print(welch_res)

get_welch_f <- function(y, groups) {
  oneway.test(y ~ groups)$statistic
}

# Generate Permutational Null Distribution for Welch's F
set.seed(123)
n_perm <- 99
welch_obs <- get_welch_f(y1, Xf)
welch_perms <- replicate(n_perm, {
  get_welch_f(y1, sample(Xf))
})

p_welch_perm <- (sum(welch_perms >= welch_obs) + 1) / (n_perm + 1)
cat("Permutational Welch's F p-value:", p_welch_perm, "\n")
```

The chunk below builds the F2 null distribution by calling `F2_adonis2()` once per permutation. This is not executed automatically, since 99 repeated calls (each re-parsing the formula and rebuilding the distance matrix) may increase the running time. 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# ==============================================================================
# 3. F2 (F2Adonis2) Univariate Implementation & Manual Null Capture
# ==============================================================================
# Get Observed F2 - Using permutations = 1 to avoid subscript errors
set.seed(123)
fit_f2 <- F2_adonis2(y1 ~ Xf, data = df1, method = "euclidean", permutations = 1, plot.dist = FALSE)
f2_obs <- fit_f2["Model", "F2"]

# Manually capture the F2 null distribution by shuffling labels and calling
# F2_adonis2() with permutations = 1 for each shuffle
cat("Generating F2 null distribution...\n")
set.seed(123)
f2_perms <- numeric(n_perm)

for(i in 1:n_perm) {
  shuffled_df <- df1
  shuffled_df$Xf <- sample(df1$Xf)
  
  tmp <- F2_adonis2(y1 ~ Xf, data = shuffled_df, method = "euclidean", permutations = 1, plot.dist = FALSE)
  f2_perms[i] <- tmp["Model", "F2"]
}

# ==============================================================================
# 4. Compare Percentiles and Distributions
# ==============================================================================
perc_welch <- mean(welch_perms <= welch_obs, na.rm = TRUE)
perc_f2    <- mean(f2_perms <= f2_obs, na.rm = TRUE)

cat("\n--- Comparison of Observed Quantiles ---\n")
cat(sprintf("Welch's F Observed Percentile: %.4f\n", perc_welch))
cat(sprintf("F2 Statistic Observed Percentile: %.4f\n", perc_f2))

null_df <- data.frame(
  Value = c(welch_perms, f2_perms),
  Test = c(rep("Welch F", length(welch_perms)), rep("F2 Stat", length(f2_perms)))
)

ggplot(null_df, aes(x = Value, fill = Test)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = welch_obs, color = "blue", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = f2_obs, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Permutational Distributions: Welch F vs F2",
       subtitle = "Dashed lines represent observed statistics",
       x = "Statistic Value", y = "Density")
```

## Case Study 1: Norway Benthic Macrofauna

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the $F_2$ statistic, we replicate the analysis of the Norway benthic macrofauna dataset (Ekofisk oil field) (Ellingsen and Gray 2002). This dataset consists of presence-absence data for 809 species across 101 sites, categorized into 5 Areas with unbalanced sample sizes.

### Load Data and Libraries

```{r}

library(F2Adonis2)

library(vegan)



# Load package datasets

data(norway_pa)

data(norway_metadata)



# Unbalanced design overview

table(norway_metadata$Area)
```

### Visualizing Dispersion Heterogeneity

Before running the test, we can confirm the presence of the Behrens-Fisher problem by visualizing the unequal group spreads using vegan::betadisper.

```{r}
dist_jaccard <- vegdist(norway_pa, method = "jaccard")

mod_disp <- betadisper(dist_jaccard, norway_metadata$Area)

# Plotting dispersions
plot(mod_disp, main = "Multivariate Dispersions (Norway Data)")


library(yarrr)

# Extract data into a frame for plotting
disp_data <- data.frame(
  Distance = mod_disp$distances,
  Area = mod_disp$group
)

# Enhanced Pirate Plot
pirateplot(formula = Distance ~ Area,
           data = disp_data,
           main = "Multivariate Dispersions (Norway Data)",
           xlab = "Geographic Area",
           ylab = "Distance to Centroid",
           theme = 1,          # Clean theme
           pal = "basel",      # Professional palette
           point.o = 0.9,      # Transparency of raw points
           avg.line.o = 0.8,   # High visibility for mean
           bean.f.o = 0.2,     # Light density bean
           inf.method = "hdi") # High-density interval for inference
```


### Global F2 PERMANOVA

We apply the F2_adonis2 function. Setting `bootstrap = TRUE` and `bias.adjust = TRUE` also reports the bootstrap and bias-adjusted bootstrap p-values alongside the permutation p-value. `permutations = 99` is used here to reduce the running time; the accompanying JOSS paper reports results at `permutations = 999`.


```{r}
set.seed(123)

# Conventional perMANOVA pseudo-F:

fit_results1 <- adonis2(

  formula = norway_pa ~ Area,

  data = norway_metadata,

  method = "jaccard",

  permutations = 99

)

fit_results1


# Running the F2 test

fit_results2 <- F2_adonis2(

  formula = norway_pa ~ Area,

  data = norway_metadata,

  method = "jaccard",

  permutations = 99,

  bootstrap = TRUE,

  bias.adjust = TRUE,

  plot.dist = FALSE

)



fit_results2
```

## Case Study 2: PKD Metabolomics

This example uses the urinary metabolomics matrix included in the package (95 samples, 1,554 metabolites), derived from the cohort in Houske et al. (2023).

```{r}
# ==============================================================================
# High-Dimensional Case Study (PKD Metabolomics)
# ==============================================================================
# Demonstrating scaling to 1,554 variables where Welch's F is unavailable.
library(dplyr)
library(F2Adonis2)

set.seed(123)

cat("\n--- Loading PKD Data ---\n")

# Load pre-packaged internal data objects
data("pkd_metadata", package = "F2Adonis2")
data("pkd_metabolites", package = "F2Adonis2")

group_labels <- factor(pkd_metadata$Group)
Y_pkd_final <- as.matrix(pkd_metabolites)

cat(sprintf("Final Processed Data: %d samples x %d metabolites\n", 
            nrow(Y_pkd_final), ncol(Y_pkd_final)))

# ==============================================================================
# PERFORM F2 ANALYSIS
# ==============================================================================
cat("\n--- Running F2 PERMANOVA ---\n")

pkd_meta <- data.frame(Group = group_labels)

# Run F2 with 99 permutations and bias-adjusted bootstrap.
# permutations = 99 is used here to keep the vignette fast to build; the
# accompanying JOSS paper reports results at permutations = 999.
pkd_f2_results <- F2_adonis2(
  formula = Y_pkd_final ~ Group,
  data = pkd_meta,
  method = "euclidean",
  permutations = 99,
  bootstrap = TRUE,
  bias.adjust = TRUE,
  plot.dist = FALSE
)

print(pkd_f2_results)
```


## Implementation Details

The F2_adonis2 function is designed to be a "drop-in" replacement for vegan::adonis2, supporting standard R formulas and distance calculations via vegdist. Key features include:

Internal Consistency: Implements the $V_i$ estimator directly from the distance matrix to handle high-dimensional compositional data.

Flexible Bootstrapping: Offers both standard permutation and separate-sample residual bootstrapping.

Bias Correction: Includes an empirical bias correction for bootstrap variances as derived in Anderson et al. (2017).

Houske, E. A., Glimm, M. G., Bergstrom, A. R., Slipher, S. K., Welhaven, H. D., Greenwood, M. C., Linse, G. M., June, R. K., Yu, A. S. L., Wallace, D. P., & Hahn, A. K. (2023).
